title: The Stories We Tell: Curriculum Design
author: Nick Hart
summary: In this installment of his Stories We Tell series, Nick Hart argues that subject leaders can use the structure of good stories, conflict, causality and complications, to help colleagues understand and remember curriculum intent. Conflict appears in the deliberate choices about content, which leaders should be able to justify at top, mid and granular levels. Causality appears in progression, where no unit is an island and concepts such as chronology or locational knowledge build year by year. Complications appear in the small components that must be mastered to reach an end point such as a perspective drawing or winning a point in badminton, and in what leaders say to do when children have not learned what was intended. Hart adds a fourth c, character, because children are the protagonists, and he concludes that subject leaders must first build deep knowledge of how the curriculum plays out before they monitor or advise.
points: Conflict in a curriculum story is the deliberate content choice, and 'we have always done it' or 'it is in the scheme' is not a reason a leader can tell a story about.
Causality shows up as conceptual progression across years, so leaders should be able to narrate how a concept such as chronology or place develops from Early Years to Year 6.
Complications are the many practised components behind each end-point task, and the key story is what happens when children have not learned: stop the conveyor belt and make time to reteach.
The lesson or the term is the wrong unit of time, because a curriculum built around a small amount of essential knowledge can flex to the time children need.
Subject leaders build the expertise to tell these stories by learning the whole curriculum and how it lands with children, which looks like monitoring but has a different purpose.
quotes: If we want colleagues to understand and remember our message in order to influence their behaviour, telling stories appears an effective way of doing so.

Perhaps all would benefit from subject leaders harnessing the power of story to build collective knowledge of their subject, using the common features of stories: conflict, causality and complications.
The importance of conflict here is that that subject leaders can bring to life the interesting decisions that they have made and justify the reasoning.
No unit is an island and each must build on what has already been learned and lay the foundations for future learning – this is the essence of a coherent curriculum.
We then provide enough interaction for them to learn it as opposed to filling a unit of work with a number of lessons. If children need more time, we make it. If they need less, we can move on.

But there is a fourth ‘c’: character. Great stories have interesting characters and our curriculum is only as good as the impact it has on children. Children are the protagonists in our curriculum stories.
Great story telling is rooted in the knowledge of the story so subject leaders need to know an awful lot to be able to do this well.
